Today we will look at an overview of the different digital tools we will use in this course. Practical topics covered include:

- Using a scientific calculator,
- Using Python as a calculator.

For this workshop you will need pen, paper, and a scientific calculator. This will take place in a computer lab so you do not need to bring your own laptop.


## Knowledge Check

Each week you have a quiz, designed to check understanding of the core calculations on a topic. To help with those who find a particular week difficult, each workshop will start with some similar questions. 

1. Euler's Constant, $e = 2.718282\ldots$, is often used when modelling growth. What is $e$ when rounded down to one significant figure? What is it when rounded up to two decimal places?

2. In a semester 1 lab, we tested how strongly we all tasted PTC. Seven students tasted it strongly, five weakly, and two not at all. What proportion of us didn't taste PTC?

3. A student scored twenty-nine out of forty marks on their project. However, they automatically  receive a $5\%$ penalty for submitting three hours after the deadline. What is their mark after the penalty is applied?

4. Kelvin is the base unit for temperature in the International Systems of Units. $273.15~\text{K}$ corresponds to $0^{\circ}\text{C}$. What is the current temperature in Kelvin?

Remember that the quiz must be submitted before the end of this tutorial.


## Rounding

We've seen how calculations often leave us with decimal places that require rounding. For each of the following scenarios, describe what system of rounding would be appropriate to use and why.

1. Measuring the distance in metres between trees in a dense orchard.
2. Weight in grams found using a set of normal kitchen scales.
3. The bill (in pounds and pence) for lab equipment when split between two departments.
4. Timing how long in minutes it takes for my bus home to arrive.
5. A student's final mark on a written exam.

:::{.callout-tip title=Hint}
Remember, you are being marked on your explanation - not just the final answer!
:::

::::{.content-hidden unless-meta=answers}
:::{.callout-note title=Solution}
Most of these don't have a single correct answer! There'll be a range of answers that are appropriate, but whether or not a specific rounding is appropriate will depend on whether the argument supports that.
:::
::::


## Ratios

In lab session 2 we did vitamin C analysis using DCPIP titration. As part of the sample preparation for the tablets we did this:

> **Step 5:** Complete a $1:100$ serial dilution of the solution you've made. Pipette $1~\text{cm}^3$ of the solution into $99~\text{ml}$ of distilled water in a $250~\text{cm}^3$ conical flask.

What is the purpose of specifying the ratio $1:100$ in this step?
